data.title: Liptovská Štiavnica – Lúčny Hríb, a hillfort on a dolomite crag
data.excerpt: An isolated dolomite crag at the mouth of the Zemianska valley, 642 m above sea level, carries a summit plateau of natural terraces that our ancestors fortified as early as the Hallstatt period. Late Hallstatt and Late La Tène finds come from the damaged rampart, while pottery decorated with a high wavy line dates the Slavic occupation to the 9th century.

mediaTexts.alt: A grassy hill with a rocky ridge and spruces, a mountain range in the background

children.text: The hillfort of Lúčny Hríb, at an elevation of 642 m above sea level, lies on a small rocky eminence in the southern part of the cadastral area of the village of Liptovská Štiavnica, at the mouth of the Zemianska valley, as an isolated dolomite crag. Some authors suggest that the name comes from the fact that the shape of the hillfort may recall the shape of a mushroom (hríb). Closer to the truth, however, is probably a name derived from the word stem „hrb“, here evidently in the sense of „a prominent hill“, which is also supported by the name of the site given on the second military survey (Luzy Wrch).

This hill rises several tens of metres above the surrounding terrain (c. 20–30). It represents the last spur of the mountain range running northwards into the Liptov Basin and has an elongated shape. The rock is a dolomitic limestone of grey and greyish-white colour, moderately weathered. It contains numerous thin calcite veins. The steep hillock is covered with a growth of grasses, with scattered shrubs and trees. A stream flows close to the hill, and in the past it played a significant part in shaping it. Thanks to the shallow soil and the fissured rock this is a very dry habitat, which probably contributed to the fact that our ancestors already lived here in the Hallstatt period, and later fortified the place and used it as a hillfort.    
 
 The archaeologist Martin Furman states that the hillfort was frequently disturbed by amateur digging and by stone quarrying, which distorts the original shaping of the rocky eminence. The western side is formed by a steep slope; to the north and east it adjoins a terrace, from which access to the summit plateau is easiest. The highest, southern point of the hillfort forms a knoll, which is continued by the steeply descending sharp ridge of the dolomite crag. The naturally delimited summit plateau is formed by terraces suitable for temporary occupation. The northern and eastern sides of the summit plateau were probably enclosed by a rampart, since it is in these parts that the difference in height between the terrace and the top of the hillfort is smallest. This is also faintly apparent in the terrain. The archaeological material known so far allows the origin of this site to be placed as early as among the hillforts of the Hallstatt period.

During archaeological work on the hillfort in 1968 and 1969, several fragments of Slavic pottery were found. In the past this find spot was disturbed by amateur digging, and a few undiagnostic finds of the Late Hallstatt and Late La Tène periods were recovered from the damaged defences. The remains of Slavic occupation were found in a thin stony layer immediately above the present-day surface. It is an assemblage of pottery fragments, among which attention is deserved by sherds decorated with a multiple high wavy line with traces of pronounced wheel-finishing, and by a fragment of a vessel with a short, as if rounded rim with a low double wavy line on the neck. Although only a few fragments of the pottery survive, its origin can be dated with certainty to the 9th century.

In 1967, during the investigation of the site by Karol Pieta, fragments of iron objects, a temple ring of bronze wire and Late La Tène pottery were found. The layer in which the objects were found lies beneath a small rampart protecting the summit plateau. Both the layer and the pottery found here bear traces of intense heat. The pottery recovered is mainly graphite ware, vertically combed, with a wide but flat rim. The find of a fragment of a wheel-thrown vessel decorated with white painting adds to the number of finds of this kind of pottery in northern Slovakia. Such finds have also been made at Batizovce and Liptovská Mara.

This natural monument is easily accessible from Ružomberok, about 10 km away. Together with a visit to the precious medieval church of All Saints before Ludrová and the manor house in Liptovská Štiavnica, it makes a rewarding destination for a short afternoon cycling trip. In summer the attraction of the place is further increased by a nearby sheepfold, where sheep cheese and žinčica (sheep whey) can be bought at a good price.
